items.question: What is Memory Chess?
items.answer: Memory Chess is a free board-memory game. You study a chess position for a short time, rebuild it from memory, and get a score based on how many pieces you placed correctly.

items.question: How do I play?
items.answer: Choose how many pieces you want and how long you want to study the board. When the position disappears, place the pieces back on the squares you remember. Submit your answer to see your accuracy and time.

items.question: Can beginners play Memory Chess?
items.answer: Yes. You do not need to know chess openings or calculate moves. Start with fewer pieces and more study time, then make the game harder when you feel ready.

items.question: How does it train chess visualization?
items.answer: Each round gives you focused practice holding a chess position in your mind and recalling where the pieces belong. Your score shows which positions feel easy and where you need more practice.

items.question: What should I look for when memorizing the board?
items.answer: Start with easy anchors such as kings, queens, corners, and edge squares. Then look for groups, lines, diagonals, and empty spaces instead of trying to remember every piece on its own.

items.question: How can I make the game harder?
items.answer: Add more pieces, shorten the study time, or hide the board coordinates. Change one setting at a time so you can see what makes the biggest difference.

items.question: Is Memory Chess free?
items.answer: Yes. You can play for free without creating an account. Adding a name to the leaderboard is optional.

items.question: How often should I practice?
items.answer: A few focused rounds on a regular schedule is a good place to start. Keep sessions short enough that you can still study each position carefully.

notebook.title: You can't improve what you never measure.
notebook.lede: Most chess practice trains decisions. Very little of it checks whether you can actually hold the board in your head. That skill sits under calculation, blindfold play and spotting tactics, and it is usually left to chance.

observation.title: Players lose track of pieces mid-calculation.
observation.body: Three moves deep, a bishop on the long diagonal quietly disappears from the picture in your head. The board in front of you was right. The one in your mind was not.

hypothesis.title: Board recall is a trainable, testable skill.
hypothesis.body: Hold a position briefly, rebuild it, check the result. Repeat with more pieces and less time. <hl>We make no claims about your brain.</hl> We give you a reading you can track.

method.title: One round, one clean number.
method.body: Study, blank board, rebuild, score. Right squares are marked, wrong squares are marked, nothing is hidden. Rounds take under a minute, so you can run many.

method.title: A round, under the microscope.
method.lede: Scroll through the five phases of a single round. The diagram updates with each step. The overlays are illustrations of the method, not recordings of anyone's attention.

study.name: Study
study.title: Look for how pieces relate.
study.body: A random position appears with a countdown. Do not try to read eight pieces one at a time. Look for pieces that touch, share a file or rank, or sit together in a corner.
study.note: Fig. overlay: dashed lines join pieces that relate. A piece with no line is on its own.

chunk.name: Chunk
chunk.title: Eight pieces become three groups.
chunk.body: Because the position is random, groups come from geometry: a cluster in a corner, a pair on a file, a piece alone. One chess-memory study estimates that people hold no more than about three chunks at a time, so three groups is a sensible target. One way to hold them is to name each one, for example “corner five”, “d-file pair”, “lone king”.
chunk.note: A is a corner cluster of 5. B is a pair on the d-file. C is the black king on c4. A chess player would call A a castled shield and B a battery. Three groups to hold, not eight.

blank.name: Blank
blank.title: The board clears.
blank.body: No pieces, no hints. Just the grid. This is the moment the round actually measures: what survived in your head after the image is gone.
blank.note: Nothing to do here but hold the three groups. Repeating their names is one way to do it.

rebuild.name: Rebuild
rebuild.title: Rebuild one group at a time.
rebuild.body: Pick a piece and tap the square where it belongs. Finish a group before you start the next. In a classic chess-recall study, players put pieces back in quick bursts separated by longer pauses, which the researchers read as the gaps between chunks. Submit when you are done.
rebuild.note: Fig. the rebuilt board before it is checked. Nothing is marked until you submit.

score.name: Score
score.title: Read the result. Run it again.
score.body: You get an accuracy score from 0 to 100% the moment you submit. Ask which group each miss came from. Here group A held except the knight, which landed one file off.
score.note: Mint is correct. Orange fill is a wrong placement (knight on e3). Orange ring is the square it belonged on (f3). 7 of 8 squares is 88%. Your next round decides whether that was a fluke.

calibrate.lede: The Medium round from the real game: {pieceCount} pieces, two kings among them, {memorizeSeconds} seconds. Then the board clears and you rebuild it. You'll get a readout card with your accuracy and recall by piece type. It works with mouse, touch and keyboard.

steps: Press start. Study the position until the meter empties.
Pick a piece from the palette, then tap a square. Tap a placed piece to remove it.
Submit. Placing more pieces than the position had lowers your accuracy, so only place what you remember.

curve.desc: Memory for new material tends to fade quickly, and each well-timed review tends to slow the fade. A daily round is a natural review slot.

meta.title: Articles on chess players and their memory
meta.description: Profiles of chess players and memory researchers. Each one gives the documented feat, the research that explains it, and a drill to try.

list.heading: Articles
list.sub: Chess players and memory researchers, one profile at a time.
list.about1: Each article follows one chess player or researcher and one question about their memory. The subject may be a player known for a feat of recall, or a researcher who measured what players remember after a few seconds.
list.about2: Every article has the same parts. A portrait comes with its photographer and licence. A fact file gives the dates, the titles and the memory feat the person is known for. The story sets that feat beside the research that explains it. A source list shows where each claim comes from. A drill at the end opens a round of Memory Chess with the piece count and viewing time the story suggests.
list.about3: The articles are researched and drafted with AI assistance from published sources such as interviews, tournament reports, books and research papers. A separate check then compares every date, number and quotation with those sources before anything is published. Where sources disagree, the article says who reported what. An anecdote that sources report only as a story is told as a story. Articles in other languages are translated from the English text with AI assistance, and each translation is checked before it goes up.
